Some Controllability Results For Linearized Compressible Navier-Stokes system.Thanks: The author is a member of an IFCAM-project, Indo-French Center for Applied Mathematics - UMI IFCAM, Bangalore, India, supported by DST - IISc - CNRS - and Université Paul Sabatier Toulouse III.

Debayan Maity Address: Centre for Applicable Mathematics, TIFR, Post Bag No. 6503, GKVK Post Office, Bangalore-560065,India. Email address: debayan@math.tifrbng.res.in
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this article, we study the null controllability of linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system in one and two dimension. We first study the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes system for non-barotropic fluid linearized around a constant steady state. We prove that the linearized system around (ρ¯,0,θ¯)(\bar{\rho},0,\bar{\theta}), with ρ¯>0,\bar{\rho}>0, θ¯>0\bar{\theta}>0 is not null controllable by localized interior control or by boundary control. But the system is null controllable by interior controls acting everywhere in the velocity and temperature equation for regular initial condition. We also prove that the the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes system for non-barotropic fluid linearized around a constant steady state (ρ¯,v¯,θ¯)(\bar{\rho},\bar{v},\bar{\theta}), with ρ¯>0,\bar{\rho}>0, v¯>0,\bar{v}>0, θ¯>0\bar{\theta}>0 is not null controllable by localized interior control or by boundary control for small time T.T. Next we consider two-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes system for barotropic fluid linearized around a constant steady state (ρ¯,𝟎).(\bar{\rho},{\bf 0}). We prove that this system is also not null controllable by localized interior control.

Key words. Linearized compressible Navier-Stokes System, Null controllability, localized interior control, boundary control, Gaussian Beam.

AMS subject classifications. 35Q30, 93C20, 93B05

1. Introduction

Control of fluid flow has been an important area of research and has many practical applications. The question about controllability of fluid flows has attracted the attention of many researchers, more for incompressible flow but much less for compressible flow. In this paper we are interested in controllability properties of linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system.

For a compressible, isothermal barotropic fluid (density is a function of only pressure), the Navier-Stokes system in Ω⊂ℝN,\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, consists of equation of continuity

∂ρ∂t​(x,t)+div​[ρ⁡(x,t)​𝐮​(t,x)]=0,\begin{array}[]{lll}\displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}(x,t)+\mbox{div}[\rho(x,t){\bf u}(t,x)]=0,\end{array} (1.1)

and the momentum equation

ρ(x,t)[∂𝐮∂t(x,t)+(𝐮(x,t).∇)𝐮(x,t)−𝐟(x,t)]=−∇p(x,t)+μ△𝐮(x,t)+(λ+μ)∇[div 𝐮(x,t)],\begin{array}[]{lll}\displaystyle\rho(x,t)\left[\frac{\partial{\bf u}}{\partial t}(x,t)+({\bf u}(x,t).\nabla){\bf u}(x,t)-{\bf f}(x,t)\right]\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle=-\nabla p(x,t)+\mu\bigtriangleup{\bf u}(x,t)+(\lambda+\mu)\nabla[\mbox{div }{\bf u}(x,t)],\end{array} (1.2)

where ρ⁡(x,t)\rho(x,t) is the density of the fluid, 𝐮⁡(x,t){\bf u}(x,t) denotes the velocity vector in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} and 𝐟⁡(x,t){\bf f}(x,t) is an external force field in ℝN.\mathbb{R}^{N}. The pressure satisfies the following constitutive law

p⁡(x,t)=a​ργ​(x,t),t>0,x∈Ω,p(x,t)=a\rho^{\gamma}(x,t),\quad t>0,\quad x\in\Omega, (1.3)

for some constants a>0a>0, γ≥1.\gamma\geq 1. The viscosity coefficients μ\mu and λ\lambda are assumed to be constant satisfying the following thermodynamic restrictions, μ>0\mu>0, λ+μ≥0.\lambda+\mu\geq 0. For non-barotropic fluid (when density is a function of pressure and temperature of the fluid), the Navier-Stokes system consists of the equation of continuity, the momentum equation and an additional thermal energy equation

cvρ(x,t)[∂θ∂t+𝐮.∇θ](x,t)+θ(x,t)∂p∂θ(x,t)div 𝐮(x,t)=κ△θ⁡(x,t)+λ​(div ​𝐮​(x,t))2+2​μ​∑i,j=1N14​(∂𝐮i∂xj+∂𝐮j∂xi)2,\begin{array}[]{lll}\displaystyle c_{v}\rho(x,t)\left[\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial t}+{\bf u}.\nabla\theta\right](x,t)+\theta(x,t)\frac{\partial p}{\partial\theta}(x,t)\mbox{div }{\bf u}(x,t)\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle=\kappa\bigtriangleup\theta(x,t)+\lambda(\mbox{div }{\bf u}(x,t))^{2}+2\mu\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{\partial{\bf u}_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}+\frac{\partial{\bf u}_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}\right)^{2},\end{array} (1.4)

where θ⁡(x,t)\theta(x,t) denotes the temperature of the fluid, cvc_{v} is the specific heat constant and κ\kappa is the heat conductivity constant. For ideal gas, the pressure is given by Boyle’s law:

p⁡(x,t)=R​ρ​(x,t)​θ​(x,t),p(x,t)=R\ \rho(x,t)\ \theta(x,t), (1.5)

where RR is the universal gas constant (See [8]).

In this article, we first consider the compressible Navier-Stokes system for non-barotropic fluid in a bounded interval (0,L),(0,L), linearized around a constant steady state (ρ¯,0,θ¯),(\bar{\rho},0,\bar{\theta}), with ρ¯>0\bar{\rho}>0 and θ¯>0.\bar{\theta}>0. More precisely we consider the system

θt−κρ¯​cv​θx​x+R​θ¯cv​ux=h​χ𝒪3, in ​(0,L)×(0,T),\displaystyle\theta_{t}-\frac{\kappa}{\bar{\rho}c_{v}}\theta_{xx}+\frac{R\bar{\theta}}{c_{v}}u_{x}\;=h\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{3}},\mbox{ in }(0,L)\times(0,T), (1.6)

where χ𝒪i\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{i}} is the characteristic function of an open subset 𝒪i⊂(0,L).{\mathcal{O}}_{i}\subset(0,L). We choose the following initial and boundary conditions for the system (1.6):

ρ(0)=ρ0,u(0)=u0 and θ(0)=θ0, in (0,L),u(0,t)=0,u(L,t)=0∀t>0,θ(0,t)=0,θ(L,t)=0∀t>0.\begin{array}[]{lll}\rho(0)=\rho_{0},\quad u(0)=u_{0}\mbox{ and }\theta(0)=\theta_{0},\mbox{ in }(0,L),\\[5.69054pt] u(0,t)=0,\quad u(L,t)=0\quad\forall\ \ t>0,\\[5.69054pt] \theta(0,t)=0,\quad\theta(L,t)=0\quad\forall\ \ t>0.\end{array} (1.7)

In (1.6) - (1.7), ff, gg and hh are distributed controls. We are interested in the following question: given T>0T>0 and (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈(L2​(0,L))3,(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in(L^{2}(0,L))^{3}, can we find interior control functions such that the solution (ρ,u,θ)(\rho,u,\theta) of (1.6) - (1.7) satisfies

(ρ,u,θ)​(x,T)=0​ for all ​x∈(0,L)​?(\rho,u,\theta)(x,T)=0\mbox{ for all }x\in(0,L)? (1.8)

Our first main result regarding interior null controllability is the following,

Theorem 1.1.

Let

𝒪1⊂(0,L),𝒪2⊆(0,L),𝒪3⊆(0,L),{\mathcal{O}}_{1}\subset(0,L),\quad{\mathcal{O}}_{2}\subseteq(0,L),\qquad{\mathcal{O}}_{3}\subseteq(0,L),

i.e., 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} is a proper subset of (0,L).(0,L). Let us assume (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L). The system (1.6) - (1.7) is not null controllable in any T>0T>0 by the interior controls f∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪1))f\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}({\mathcal{O}}_{1})), g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪2))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}({\mathcal{O}}_{2})) and h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪3))h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}({\mathcal{O}}_{3})) acting on density, velocity and temperature equation respectively.

Remark 1.2.

The above negative result can be extended to the case of less regular interior controls or boundary control. See Remark 2.14 and Remark 2.15 for more details.

Our next positive result shows that, if initial density ρ0\rho_{0} lies in a more regular space then the linearized system is null controllable by velocity and temperature controls acting everywhere in the domain.

Theorem 1.3.

Let f≡0f\equiv 0 in (1.6). Let us denote

Hm1​(0,L)={ρ∈H1​(0,L)|∫01ρ⁡(x)​𝑑x=0}.H^{1}_{m}(0,L)=\left\{\rho\in H^{1}(0,L)|\int_{0}^{1}\rho(x)dx=0\right\}.

Let us assume (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈Hm1​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in H^{1}_{m}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L). Then for any T>0,T>0, there exist controls g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,L))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,L)) and h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,L))h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,L)) acting everywhere in the velocity and temperature equation respectively, such that the solution of (1.6) - (1.7) satisfies

(ρ,u,θ)​(x,T)=0​ for all ​x∈(0,L).(\rho,u,\theta)(x,T)=0\mbox{ for all }x\in(0,L).

The next result shows that the above result is sharp as null controllability cannot be achieved by localized interior velocity and temperature controls.

Theorem 1.4.

Let f≡0f\equiv 0 in (1.6). Let

𝒪2⊂(0,L),𝒪3⊆(0,L),{\mathcal{O}}_{2}\subset(0,L),\qquad{\mathcal{O}}_{3}\subseteq(0,L),

i.e., 𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{2} is a proper subset of (0,L).(0,L). Let us assume (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈Hm1​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in H^{1}_{m}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L). The system (1.6) - (1.7) is not null controllable in any T>0T>0 by the interior controls g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪2))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}({\mathcal{O}}_{2})) and h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪3)),h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}({\mathcal{O}}_{3})), acting on velocity and temperature equation respectively.

The proof of these results relies on the observability inequality. We know that the null controllability of a linear system is equivalent to a certain observability inequality for the solutions of adjoint system (see [6], Chapter 2). To prove the negative results, we will construct particular solutions for the adjoint system such that the observability inequality cannot hold. In order to do that first we will consider the adjoint system in ℝ×(0,T)\mathbb{R}\times(0,T) as a terminal value problem. We will construct highly localized solutions known as “Gaussian Beam”. Similar kind of construction has been used for hyperbolic equations by Ralston ([13]) and for wave equations by Macià and Zuazua ([9]). We will prove that solutions are localized in a small neighbourhood of any x0∈ℝ.x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}. Thus given an observation set, we can always find an interval away from the observation set such that the solutions are localized in that interval. Using this we are able to prove the negative results. To the author’s best knowledge these are new results regarding controllability issues of Navier-Stokes system for non-barotropic fluid.

In Theorem 1.4, we proved a positive result when controls acting everywhere in the equation. The question then arises: whether positive results could be obtained by using control supported in a small, but moving region, as in [10, 2]. Rosier and Rouchon in [15] proved that the structurally damped wave equation in one dimension is not null controllable by a boundary control. Later on Martin, Rosier and Rouchon in [10] proved that the same equation in one dimension with periodic boundary conditions, is null controllable with a moving distributed control for sufficiently large time. Chaves-Silva, Rosier and Zuazua in [2] extend the above result to higher dimension. The structure of the system considered by the authors in [10, 2], in some sense, is similar to the linearized compressible, barotropic Navier-Stokes system in one dimension as well as in higher dimension. These issues will be discussed in a future work which is in progress.

We have studied in this paper the null controllability of the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system only. The “Gaussian Beam” construction is used to show negative results. However one may use other techniques based on the use of nonlinearity (see [6] for example) to achieve controllability results for the full nonlinear system.

There have been some results regarding the control of compressible barotropic fluid models in recent years. Amosova in [1] considers compressible Navier-Stokes system for viscous barotropic fluid in one dimension in Lagrangian coordinates in a bounded domain (0,1)(0,1) with Dirichlet boundary condition. She proves local exact controllability to trajectories for the velocity in any time T>0,T>0, using a localized interior control on the velocity equation, provided that the initial density is already on the targeted trajectory and initial condition lies in H1​(0,1)×H01​(0,1).H^{1}(0,1)\times H^{1}_{0}(0,1).

Ervedoza, Glass, Guerrero and Puel in [7] consider the compressible Navier-Stokes system in one space dimension in a bounded domain (0,L)(0,L). They prove local exact controllability to constant states (ρ¯,u¯)(\bar{\rho},\bar{u}) with ρ¯>0,u¯≠0\bar{\rho}>0,\bar{u}\neq 0 using two boundary controls, both for density and velocity, in time T>L|u¯|\displaystyle T>\frac{L}{|\bar{u}|} when initial condition lies in H3​(0,L)×H3​(0,L).H^{3}(0,L)\times H^{3}(0,L).

Chowdhury, Ramaswamy and Raymond in [5] consider the compressible barotropic Navier-Stokes system linearized around a constant steady state (Q0,0)(Q_{0},0) with Q0>0Q_{0}>0 in a bounded domain (0,π)(0,\pi). They proved that the linearized system is not null controllable by a localized control or by boundary control. They also proved that the linearized system is null controllable by an interior control acting everywhere in the velocity equation when initial condition lies in Hm1​(0,π)×L2​(0,π).H^{1}_{m}(0,\pi)\times L^{2}(0,\pi).

Chowdhury in [3] considers the compressible barotropic Navier-Stokes system linearized about a constant steady state (Q0,V0)(Q_{0},V_{0}) with Q0>0,V0>0Q_{0}>0,V_{0}>0 in (0,L)(0,L) with Dirichlet boundary condition and an interior control on the velocity equation acting on open subset (0,l)⊂(0,L).(0,l)\subset(0,L). He proves that the system is approximately controllable in L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L) when T>L−lV0.\displaystyle T>\frac{L-l}{V_{0}}. He also proves a similar result in two dimension.

Chowdhury, Mitra, Ramaswamy and Renardy in [4] consider the compressible barotropic Navier-Stokes system linearized about a constant steady state (Q0,V0)(Q_{0},V_{0}) with Q0>0,V0>0Q_{0}>0,V_{0}>0 in (0,2​π)(0,2\pi) with periodic boundary condition. They proved that the linearized system is null controllable by a localized velocity control when T>2​πV0\displaystyle T>\frac{2\pi}{V_{0}} and initial condition lies in Hm1​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π).H^{1}_{m}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi).

Our linearized system (1.6) - (1.7) is similar to the linearized system considered by the authors in [5]. So we expect similar controllability results. Their method is based on explicit expression for eigenfunctions and the behaviour of the spectrum of the linearized operator. They proved that there is an accumulation point in the spectrum of the linearized operator. This system behaves very badly with respect to controllability properties and a similar type of controllability behaviour is also observed in [15, 11, 14] for different types of systems where an accumulation point is present in the spectrum of linearized operator. But the method used in [5] does not seem to fit very well in our case. In fact one can prove that there is an accumulation point in the spectrum of the linearized operator considered here, for certain boundary condition. But the expressions of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are complicated. So here we use Gaussian Beam approach to achieve the negative results. This technique does not require the knowledge of the spectrum and it seems to extend to higher dimension also.

The controllability properties are completely different, if we consider compressible Navier-Stokes system linearized around non null velocity. For barotropic fluid, the system linearized around (Q0,0)(Q_{0},0) is not controllable in any time TT by localized interior control but the system linearized around (Q0,V0)(Q_{0},V_{0}) is null controllable by localized interior control for large time T.T. It is interesting to note that there is no accumulation point in the spectrum of the linearized operator in the latter case and better controllability behaviour at least for TT large enough(see [4]). But the question remains what happens when time TT is small enough. Our results answer this question in the negative.

We consider the compressible non-barotropic Navier-Stokes equation linearized around constant steady state (ρ¯,v¯,θ¯),(\bar{\rho},\bar{v},\bar{\theta}), ρ¯>0,v¯>0,θ¯>0\bar{\rho}>0,\bar{v}>0,\bar{\theta}>0

ρt+v¯​ρx+ρ¯​ux=f​χ𝒪1, in ​(0,L)×(0,T),ut−λ+2​μρ¯​ux​x+R​θ¯ρ¯​ρx+v¯​ux+R​θx=g​χ𝒪2, in ​(0,L)×(0,T),θt​(x,t)−κρ¯​cv​θx​x+R​θ¯cv​ux+v¯​θx=h​χ𝒪3, in ​(0,L)×(0,T),ρ(0)=ρ0,u(0)=u0, and θ(0)=θ0, in (0,L),ρ(0,t)=0,u(0,t)=0=u(L,t),∀t∈(0,T),θ(0,t)=0=θ(L,t),∀t∈(0,T).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\rho_{t}+\bar{v}\rho_{x}+\bar{\rho}\;u_{x}\;\;=f\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{1}},\mbox{ in }(0,L)\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle u_{t}-\frac{\lambda+2\mu}{\bar{\rho}}u_{xx}+\frac{R\bar{\theta}}{\bar{\rho}}\;\rho_{x}+\bar{v}u_{x}+R\theta_{x}\;=g\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{2}},\mbox{ in }(0,L)\times(0,T),\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle\theta_{t}(x,t)-\frac{\kappa}{\bar{\rho}c_{v}}\theta_{xx}+\frac{R\bar{\theta}}{c_{v}}u_{x}+\bar{v}\theta_{x}\;=h\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{3}},\mbox{ in }(0,L)\times(0,T),\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle\rho(0)=\rho_{0},\quad\quad u(0)=u_{0},\mbox{ and }\quad\theta(0)=\theta_{0},\quad\mbox{ in }(0,L),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle\rho(0,t)=0,\;\;\;u(0,t)=0=u(L,t),\;\;\forall\ t\in(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle\theta(0,t)=0=\theta(L,t),\;\;\forall\ t\in(0,T).\end{array} (1.9)

We prove the following theorem.

Theorem 1.5.

Let

𝒪1=(l1,l2)⊂(0,L),𝒪2⊆(0,L)𝒪3⊆(0,L),{\mathcal{O}}_{1}=(l_{1},l_{2})\subset(0,L),\quad{\mathcal{O}}_{2}\subseteq(0,L)\quad{\mathcal{O}}_{3}\subseteq(0,L),

i.e., 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} is a proper subset of (0,L).(0,L). Let us assume (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L). If T<max⁡{l1v¯,L−l2v¯},\displaystyle T<\max\left\{\frac{l_{1}}{\bar{v}},\frac{L-l_{2}}{\bar{v}}\right\}, then the system (1.9) is not null controllable by localized interior controls f∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪1)),f\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{1})), g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪2))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}({\mathcal{O}}_{2})) and h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪3))h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}({\mathcal{O}}_{3})) acting on density, velocity and temperature equation respectively.

As a corollary of the above Theorem, one can rule out null controllability of compressible barotropic Navier-Stokes system linearized around constant steady state (ρ¯,v¯)(\bar{\rho},\bar{v}) in small time T,T, using a boundary control or localized interior control.

Corollary 1.6.

We consider compressible barotropic Navier-Stokes system linearized around a constant steady state (ρ¯,v¯)(\bar{\rho},\bar{v}), ρ¯>0,v¯>0\bar{\rho}>0,\bar{v}>0 in (0,L)×(0,T)(0,L)\times(0,T) or in (0,2​π)×(0,T)(0,2\pi)\times(0,T) as in [4, 3].

  • (i)

    For initial condition belonging to L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L),L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L), the system with Dirichlet boundary condition is not null controllable at any time T>0T>0 by a interior control acting only in the velocity equation. The control may act in a non empty open subset of (0,L)(0,L) or in the whole domain (0,L).(0,L).

  • (ii)

    The system with periodic boundary condition is not null controllable by interior control localized in (l1,l2)⊂(0,2​π),(l_{1},l_{2})\subset(0,2\pi), acting only in the velocity equation when initial condition lies in Hm1​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)H^{1}_{m}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi) and time T<max⁡{l1v¯,2​π−l2v¯}.\displaystyle T<\max\left\{\frac{l_{1}}{\bar{v}},\frac{2\pi-l_{2}}{\bar{v}}\right\}.

  • (iii)

    For initial condition belonging to L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L),L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L), the same system is not null controllable by boundary control if time T<Lv¯.\displaystyle T<\frac{L}{\bar{v}}.

Remark 1.7.

From the above corollary we see that the condition T>L|v¯|T>\displaystyle\frac{L}{|\bar{v}|} in Ervedoza,Glass,Guerrero and Puel ([7]) is natural.

Next we will show that, our method can be extended to higher dimension also. For simplicity we consider the compressible barotropic Navier-Stokes system in two-dimensional bounded domain Ω\Omega, linearized around a constant steady state solution (ρ¯,0,0)(\bar{\rho},0,0) , ρ¯>0,\bar{\rho}>0,

ρt+ρ¯​div​𝐮=f​χ𝒪1, in ​Ω×(0,T),𝐮−μρ¯Δ𝐮−λ+μρ¯∇[div𝐮]+aγρ¯γ−2∇ρ=𝐠χ𝒪2, in Ω×(0,T),ρ⁡(0)=ρ0and𝐮⁡(0)=𝐮0, in ​Ω,𝐮=𝟎 on ​∂Ω×(0,T).\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\rho_{t}+\bar{\rho}\ \mathrm{div}\;{\bf u}\;\;=f\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{1}},\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle{\bf u}-\frac{\mu}{\bar{\rho}}\Delta{\bf u}-\frac{\lambda+\mu}{\bar{\rho}}\nabla[\mathrm{div}\ {\bf u}]+\;a\gamma\bar{\rho}^{\gamma-2}\nabla\rho\;=\;{\bf g}\chi_{{\mathcal{O}}_{2}},\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle\rho(0)=\rho_{0}\quad\mbox{and}\quad{\bf u}(0)={\bf u}_{0},\quad\mbox{ in }\Omega,\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle{\bf u}={\bf 0}\ \ \mbox{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T).\end{array} (1.10)

where 𝐮=(u1,u2){\bf u}=(u_{1},u_{2}) and 𝒪1,𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2} are open subsets of Ω.\Omega. We obtain the following negative null controllability result for the system (1.10).

Theorem 1.8.

Let

𝒪1⊂Ω,𝒪2⊆Ω,\mathcal{O}_{1}\subset\Omega,\quad\mathcal{O}_{2}\subseteq\Omega,

i.e., 𝒪1\mathcal{O}_{1} is a proper open subset of Ω.\Omega. Let us assume that (ρ0,𝐮0)∈(L2​(Ω))3.(\rho_{0},{\bf u}_{0})\in(L^{2}(\Omega))^{3}. Then the system (1.10) is not null controllable in time any T>0T>0 by interior controls f∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪1))f\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{1})) and 𝐠∈(L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪2)))2.{\bf g}\in(L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{2})))^{2}.

The plan of the paper is as follows. In section 2, we study the control system linearized around a constant steady state (ρ¯,0,θ¯)(\bar{\rho},0,\bar{\theta}) in one dimension. We prove Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.3 and Theorem 1.4 here. In section 3, we study the control system linearized around a constant steady state (ρ¯,v¯,θ¯).(\bar{\rho},\bar{v},\bar{\theta}). Theorem 1.5 is proved here. In section 4 we consider the linearized system in two dimension around constant steady state (ρ¯,𝟎).(\bar{\rho},{\bf 0}). We prove Theorem 1.8 here.

2. Null Controllability of Compressible Non-Barotropic Navier Stokes System in One Dimension Linearized about (ρ¯,0,θ¯)(\bar{\rho},0,\bar{\theta})

In this section, we will discuss interior null controllability of the system (1.6) - (1.7). We introduce the positive constants

g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪2))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{2})) and h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪3))h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{3})). Proof.

By a density argument we deduce that for any (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈Z(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in Z and (σT,vT,ϕT)∈Z(\sigma_{T},v_{T},\phi_{T})\in Z the identity (2.3) holds. One can use the identity (2.4) to get an observability inequality which is also equivalent to null controllability. More precisely we have the following Proposition (See [12] Section 2 and [6] Chapter 2 ).

The system (1.6) - (1.7) is null controllable in ZZ in time T>0T>0 if and only if there exists a constant CC such that for any terminal condition (σT,vT,ϕT)∈Z(\sigma_{T},v_{T},\phi_{T})\in Z, (σ,v,ϕ)(\sigma,v,\phi), the solution of the adjoint problem (2.2) satisfies the following observability inequality

≤C⁡(∫0T∫𝒪1σ2​𝑑x​𝑑t+∫0T∫𝒪2v2​𝑑x​𝑑t+∫0T∫𝒪3ϕ2​𝑑x​𝑑t).\displaystyle\leq C\left(\int_{0}^{T}\int_{{\mathcal{O}}_{1}}\sigma^{2}dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{{\mathcal{O}}_{2}}v^{2}dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{{\mathcal{O}}_{3}}\phi^{2}dxdt\right). (2.5)

Proof.

The eigenvalues of A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) are given by the roots of the characteristic polynomial

Since it is a polynomial of degree three, it will always have a real root.

Now the polynomial λ3+a​λ2+b​λ+c\lambda^{3}+a\lambda^{2}+b\lambda+c is stable i.e. all the roots have negative real part if and only if

(Theorem 2.4, Part I of [16]). For our case,

And it is easy to verify that a⁡(ξ)​b​(ξ)>c⁡(ξ)a(\xi)\ b(\xi)>c(\xi) for all ξ∈ℝ∖{0}\xi\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}. So all the eigenvalues have negative real part for all ξ∈ℝ∖{0}\xi\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}. For ξ=0,\xi=0, the characteristic polynomial has only one root 0.0.

Let {−λ⁡(ξ),−μ⁡(ξ),−δ⁡(ξ)}\{-\lambda(\xi),\,-\mu(\xi),\,-\delta(\xi)\}, be the eigenvalues of A⁡(ξ),A(\xi), given by the formula (2.11). Thus

Re​λ​(ξ)≥0,Re​μ​(ξ)≥0,Re​δ​(ξ)>0​ for all ​ξ∈ℝ∖{0}.\mathrm{Re}\ \lambda(\xi)\geq 0,\quad\mathrm{Re}\ \mu(\xi)\geq 0,\quad\mathrm{Re}\ \delta(\xi)>0\mbox{ for all }\xi\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}.

{λ⁡(ξ)+μ⁡(ξ)+δ⁡(ξ)=(ν0+k0)​ξ2,λ⁡(ξ)​μ​(ξ)+μ⁡(ξ)​δ​(ξ)+δ⁡(ξ)​λ​(ξ)=R​θ¯​ξ2+R2​b​ξ2+k0​ν0​ξ4,λ⁡(ξ)​μ​(ξ)​δ​(ξ)=k0​R​θ¯​ξ4.\displaystyle\begin{cases}&\lambda(\xi)+\mu(\xi)+\delta(\xi)=(\nu_{0}+k_{0})\xi^{2},\\ &\lambda(\xi)\mu(\xi)+\mu(\xi)\delta(\xi)+\delta(\xi)\lambda(\xi)=R\bar{\theta}\xi^{2}+R^{2}b\xi^{2}+k_{0}\nu_{0}\xi^{4},\\ &\lambda(\xi)\mu(\xi)\delta(\xi)=k_{0}R\bar{\theta}\xi^{4}.\end{cases} (2.14)

It is well known that, if the discriminant D>0,D>0, then the polynomial has three distinct real roots and if D<0,D<0, then the equation has one real root and two complex conjugate roots. In our case the discriminant is

+2(ν0+k0)2(Rθ¯+R2b)k0ν0−12(Rθ¯+R2b)k02ν02]ξ10+O(ξ8).\displaystyle\left.+2(\nu_{0}+k_{0})^{2}(R\bar{\theta}+R^{2}b)k_{0}\nu_{0}-12(R\bar{\theta}+R^{2}b)k_{0}^{2}\nu_{0}^{2}\right]\xi^{10}+O(\xi^{8}). (2.15)

Using the above theorem now we can prove Theorem 1.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Proof.

Theorem 2.13 shows, in the observability inequality (2.5), L.H.S >18​π​e−2​a1​T>\displaystyle\frac{1}{8\pi}e^{-2a_{1}T} and R.H.S ≤C​ϵ.\leq C\sqrt{\epsilon}. Hence (2.5) cannot hold. Hence system (1.6) - (1.7) is not null controllable. ∎

Remark 2.14.

The above result is established when f∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪1))f\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{1})), g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪2))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{2})) and h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪3))h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{3})). We can extend this negative result to less regular control. More precisely we can take g∈L2​(0,T,H−1​(𝒪2))g\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{-1}(\mathcal{O}_{2})) and h∈L2​(0,T,H−1​(𝒪3)).h\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{-1}(\mathcal{O}_{3})). In order to give a sense to the R.H.S. of (2.3), we need to replace χ𝒪2\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{2}} and χ𝒪3\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{3}} in (1.6) by Ψ2∈Cc∞​(𝒪2)\Psi_{2}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) and Ψ3∈Cc∞​(𝒪3)\Psi_{3}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathcal{O}_{3}) respectively. The observability inequality becomes

‖σ⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L)2+‖v⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L)2+‖ϕ⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L)2\displaystyle\|\sigma(\cdot,0)\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,L)}+\|v(\cdot,0)\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,L)}+\|\phi(\cdot,0)\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,L)}
≤C⁡(∫0T∫𝒪1σ2​𝑑x​𝑑t+∫0T∫𝒪2(Ψ2​v)x2​𝑑x​𝑑t+∫0T∫𝒪3(Ψ3​ϕ)x2​𝑑x​𝑑t)\displaystyle\leq C\left(\int_{0}^{T}\int_{{\mathcal{O}}_{1}}\sigma^{2}dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{{\mathcal{O}}_{2}}(\Psi_{2}v)_{x}^{2}dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{{\mathcal{O}}_{3}}(\Psi_{3}\phi)_{x}^{2}dxdt\right) (2.49)

where (σ,v,ϕ)(\sigma,v,\phi) is the solution of the adjoint system (2.2). Using the same construction as above one can prove that this observability inequality does not hold and hence the system is not null controllable.

Remark 2.15.

One can use the above Gaussian Beam construction to rule out null controllability using a boundary control. Let us consider the system (1.6) - (1.7) with f=g=h=0f=g=h=0 and v⁡(L,t)=q⁡(t)∈L2​(0,T).v(L,t)=q(t)\in L^{2}(0,T). In this case null controllability is equivalent to the following observability inequality

‖σ⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L)2+‖v⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L)2+‖ϕ⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L)2≤C​∫0T|R​ρ¯​θ¯​σ​(L,t)+ρ¯2​ν0​vx​(L,t)|2​𝑑t.\displaystyle\|\sigma(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{2}(0,L)}^{2}+\|v(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{2}(0,L)}^{2}+\|\phi(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{2}(0,L)}^{2}\leq C\int_{0}^{T}|R\bar{\rho}\bar{\theta}\sigma(L,t)+\bar{\rho}^{2}\nu_{0}v_{x}(L,t)|^{2}\ dt. (2.50)

where (σ,v,ϕ)(\sigma,v,\phi) is the solution of the adjoint system (2.2). We can use the above construction to show that the above observability inequality does not hold and hence the system is not null controllable by a boundary control in any time T>0T>0.

We proved that the system (1.6) - (1.7) is not null controllable when initial condition lies in ZZ. So the natural question is if the system is null controllable or not when the initial conditions are regular. In case of barotropic fluid, if initial density lies in Hm1​(0,L)H^{1}_{m}(0,L) then the system is null controllable (See [5] and [4]). In this section we choose (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈Hm1​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in H^{1}_{m}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L). We will first show that (1.6) - (1.7) is null controllable by velocity and temperature control only (i.e. when f≡0f\equiv 0) acting everywhere in the domain with this initial regular condition. Then we will show that we cannot achieve null controllability by localizing velocity and temperature control.

We consider the following interior control system

ρt+ρ¯​ux=0, in ​(0,L)×(0,T),ut−ν0​ux​x+R​θ¯ρ¯​ρx+R​θx=g​χ𝒪2, in ​(0,L)×(0,T),θt−k0​θx​x+R​θ¯cv​ux=h​χ𝒪3, in ​(0,L)×(0,T),ρ(0)=ρ0,u(0)=u0,θ(0)=θ0, in (0,L)u⁡(0,t)=0=u⁡(L,t)∀t>0,θ⁡(0,t)=0=θ⁡(L,t)∀t>0.\begin{array}[]{lll}\rho_{t}+\bar{\rho}\;u_{x}\;\;=0,\mbox{ in }(0,L)\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle u_{t}-\nu_{0}u_{xx}+\frac{R\bar{\theta}}{\bar{\rho}}\;\rho_{x}+R\theta_{x}\;=g\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{2}},\mbox{ in }(0,L)\times(0,T),\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle\theta_{t}-k_{0}\theta_{xx}+\frac{R\bar{\theta}}{c_{v}}u_{x}\;=h\chi_{\mathcal{O}_{3}},\ \mbox{ in }(0,L)\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle\rho(0)=\rho_{0},\quad u(0)=u_{0},\quad\theta(0)=\theta_{0},\mbox{ in }(0,L)\\[5.69054pt] u(0,t)=0=u(L,t)\quad\forall\ \ t>0,\quad\theta(0,t)=0=\theta(L,t)\quad\forall\ \ t>0.\end{array} (2.51)

Here gg and hh are velocity and temperature control respectively. Let us first explain why we need average zero condition for initial density. Integrating the density equation of (2.51) in (0,L)(0,L) and using the boundary conditions we deduce that

dd​t​(∫0Lρ⁡(x,t)​𝑑x)=0.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\int_{0}^{L}\rho(x,t)dx\right)=0.

Therefore

∫0Lρ⁡(x,T)​𝑑x=∫0Lρ0​(x)​𝑑x.\int_{0}^{L}\rho(x,T)dx=\int_{0}^{L}\rho_{0}(x)dx. (2.52)

∫0Lρ0​(x)​𝑑x=0.\int_{0}^{L}\rho_{0}(x)dx=0. (2.53)

Let us define

V=Hm1​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L).V=H^{1}_{m}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L).

We have the following lemma about existence and uniqueness of solution to the system (2.51) follows easily from semigroup theory.

Lemma 2.16.

Given (ρ0,u0,θ0)∈V,(\rho_{0},u_{0},\theta_{0})\in V, g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,L))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,L)) and h∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,L)),h\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,L)), the system (2.51) has a unique solution (ρ,u,θ)(\rho,u,\theta) with ρ∈L2​(0,T,Hm1​(0,L))\rho\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}_{m}(0,L)) and (u,θ)∈(L2​(0,T,H01​(0,L)))2.(u,\theta)\in(L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}_{0}(0,L)))^{2}. Proof.

satisfies

−σt+ρ¯​v=0, in ​ℝ×(0,T),−vt−ν0​vx​x+R​θ¯ρ¯​σx​x−R​ϕx=0, in ​ℝ×(0,T),−ϕt−k0​ϕx​x−R​θ¯cv​ϕx=0, in ​ℝ×(0,T),σ(T)=σT,v(T)=vT,ϕ(T)=ϕT, in ℝ.\begin{array}[]{lll}-\sigma_{t}+\bar{\rho}\;v\;\;=0,\mbox{ in }\mathbb{R}\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle-v_{t}-\nu_{0}v_{xx}+\frac{R\bar{\theta}}{\bar{\rho}}\;\sigma_{xx}-R\phi_{x}\;=0,\mbox{ in }\mathbb{R}\times(0,T),\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle-\phi_{t}-k_{0}\phi_{xx}-\frac{R\bar{\theta}}{c_{v}}\phi_{x}\;=0,\mbox{ in }\mathbb{R}\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle\sigma(T)=\sigma_{T},\quad v(T)=v_{T},\quad\phi(T)=\phi_{T},\mbox{ in }\mathbb{R}.\end{array} (2.61)

Proof.

We will proceed in a similar way as in Theorem 2.13. In order to obtain a cotradiction to the observability inequality (3.2), we need (x⁡(t)−η,x⁡(t)+η)⊂(0,L)(x(t)-\eta,x(t)+\eta)\subset(0,L) and does not intersect the set 𝒪1=(l1,l2)\mathcal{O}_{1}=(l_{1},l_{2}) for all t.t. This implies T<l1v¯.\displaystyle T<\frac{l_{1}}{\bar{v}}. Similarly if we choose x0∈(l2,L)x_{0}\in(l_{2},L) then we need T<L−l2v¯.\displaystyle T<\frac{L-l_{2}}{\bar{v}}.

Thus when T<max⁡{l1v¯,L−l2v¯},\displaystyle T<\max\left\{\frac{l_{1}}{\bar{v}},\frac{L-l_{2}}{\bar{v}}\right\}, the observability inequality (3.2) does not hold and hence the system is not null controllable. ∎

Proof.

(4.8)

Remark 4.4.

Now we can proceed as before to prove Theorem 1.8.
